title: Sleep in peace
hook: the eleven blessings of metta, read whole

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahapajapati's brief teaching, and your line: where does this lead? Today closes the week, fittingly, at bedtime.

Two in the morning, and the day is replaying: what they said, what you should have said. The last sutta of the week speaks to that hour. It comes from the final book of the Numbered Sayings, the Book of Elevens, and it lists what happens to a person who practices loving-kindness, metta, steadily: developed, cultivated, made a vehicle and a foundation, the text says, well established and well undertaken. There are eleven blessings, and today we read the whole list.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `THE BOOK OF ELEVENS.` → `ELEVEN BLESSINGS, WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in order. One: you sleep easily. Two: you wake easily. Three: you don't have bad dreams. Four: you are dear to human beings. Five: you are dear to non-human beings. Six: the devas, the gods, protect you. Seven: fire, poison and weapons don't touch you. Eight: your mind becomes concentrated quickly. Nine: your face is bright and clear. Ten: you die unconfused. Eleven: if you go no further in this life, you are reborn in the Brahma world. Notice where the list starts: not with heaven, with sleep. The first three blessings are about the night, where resentment and worry do their best work. A heart that's practiced goodwill has less to replay. Then the list moves outward, to people, to unseen beings, to protection; then inward, to concentration and a clear face; and finally to the very end, dying without confusion. A whole life, from tonight's pillow to the last breath. Some of the blessings, like fire and poison not touching you, are read by some teachers literally, as the power of a mind full of kindness, and by others as describing a life that makes fewer enemies. The text itself simply lists them. And it ties the week together: grudges removed, winds passing, less wanting, all of it makes for a quieter night.
screen: `SLEEP EASY, WAKE EASY.` · `DEAR TO HUMANS AND NON-HUMANS.` · `A QUICK MIND, A BRIGHT FACE.` · then, large: `DIE UNCONFUSED.`

segments.voice: Breathe slowly and wish yourself well in a few simple words, may I be well, may I rest; then someone you love; then someone neutral, a face you passed today; then, if you can, someone from this week's grudges. Then everyone, everywhere, going to sleep tonight, the words getting softer as you go. You can do it now, or keep it for your pillow tonight.
metta. The Pali word for loving-kindness, the practice behind the eleven blessings in the Book of Elevens, a list that runs from an easy night to an unconfused death and beyond. Today's word.
Your line: wish one person well. Eleven blessings, and the first is a good night's sleep. A week done; sleep well.

howItsDone: In some Theravada communities the eleven blessings of metta are chanted in Pali, and metta meditation, wishing well to oneself and then widening circles of beings, is a common practice before sleep.

chat.says: Does loving-kindness practice actually do anything for the person doing it?
options: The Book of Elevens lists eleven blessings, starting with sleeping easily and waking easily.
Nothing for you; the sutta says metta only benefits the person it's sent to.
Its one blessing is rebirth in heaven; this life isn't touched at all, the sutta says.
chat.meaning: AN 11.16 lists eleven blessings of steady metta, beginning with sleeping easily, waking easily and no bad dreams, and ending with an unconfused death and beyond.

metta.meaning: loving-kindness, a wish for others' good

Brahma world.meaning: a high heavenly realm in the Buddhist picture

notes: AN 11.16 paraphrased. Confirm the order of the eleven, especially 'devas protect' (6) and 'fire, poison, weapons' (7). Some editions number this AN 11.15.
The literal vs. figurative reading of blessing 7 is presented as a range of teachers' views; confirm fair.
Confirm the full list of verbs in the introductory formula.
The practice uses 'may I be well, may I rest' as simple well-wishing phrases, not a quoted prayer; confirm acceptable.
